# Cartographer · a map of how you build with coding agents
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/
Description: Cartographer reads the session history your coding agent keeps and tells it back as a story: what you did, what happened, what it meant. Local and private.

## One line to install

Mac and Linux (Terminal):

curl -fsSL https://codecartographer.dev/install.sh | sh{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Windows (PowerShell):

irm https://codecartographer.dev/install.ps1 | iex{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Needs Python 3.9+ and Claude Code. Step by step, in plain language and in detail, on the Install page.

## What you get

| Command | | When | | What you get back |

| /wrap | | End of a session | | A write-up of what you asked for, what the agent did, where things went sideways, and how you got back on track.Each point links to the moment in the transcript it came from.
In Claude Code →

|

| replay | | Any time | | The whole project, played back one step at a time.Underneath: coaching, the prompts worth keeping, and where your time actually went.
Open the demo ↗

|

| /complete | | When a version ships | | The whole build next to what you said "done" would mean.What got you there, and what it cost.
How it works →

|

## About

Cartographer is for people who code with AI: engineers who work with an agent every day, and yes, even vibe coders. It's meant to help you understand your own process, and what your projects look like in practice, session by session.

There are only so many words you can remember, and only so many prompts. A few weeks into a build, it's hard to say which prompts did the work and which ones sent the agent in circles. Cartographer isn't a prompt library, and it isn't trying to replace one. It shows you how you've been using your prompts, and how well your natural language held up against the code the AI generated.

---

# Install · Cartographer
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/install
Description: Install Claude Code, then Cartographer, in one line each. Plain-language and technical steps, manual install, update, uninstall.

## Step 1 · Claude Code

Skip this if you already type claude in a terminal. Cartographer reads the history Claude Code keeps, so Claude Code has to be there first.

Mac and Linux (Terminal):

curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Windows (PowerShell):

irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Then open a new terminal, type claude --version to check it is there, go to a project folder, type claude and press Enter: a browser window opens to sign in (a Claude subscription or an API key). claude doctor checks the install; claude update updates it. Windows: install Git for Windows too (winget install Git.Git); it gives Claude Code its Bash tool and gives Cartographer Git Bash. Other ways in: brew install --cask claude-code, winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode, or npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code with Node 22+. The official steps live at code.claude.com/docs.

## Step 2 · Cartographer

Mac and Linux (Terminal):

curl -fsSL https://codecartographer.dev/install.sh | sh{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Windows (PowerShell):

irm https://codecartographer.dev/install.ps1 | iex{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Plain language

### If you don't live in a terminal

- Open a terminal. Mac: press ⌘ Space, type Terminal, Enter. Windows: press the Windows key, type PowerShell, Enter. A window with a blinking cursor appears.

- Paste the line for your system and press Enter. It prints what it is doing. Thirty seconds, no questions. If it says Python is missing: on a Mac run xcode-select --install; on Windows run winget install Python.Python.3.12; then open a new terminal and paste the line again.

- Open your dashboard. Type cartographer serve --open and press Enter. A page opens in your browser. Only your computer can see it.

- Answer six questions. How comfortable you are with code, how experienced with prompting, what the map should sound like. This decides how Cartographer speaks to you. You can change it any time.

- Work in Claude Code as usual. Cartographer does nothing during the session.

- At the end of a session, type /wrap. Claude writes the map and tells you where the replay is. Come back to the dashboard, or type cartographer open, to watch it.

Technical

### What the script does, exactly

- Checks for python3 3.9+. Nothing else is required. No pip, no venv, no npm.

- Downloads cartographer.tar.gz from this site (built from main on every deploy), falling back to git clone.

- Runs bin/cartographer install --agent claude-code. That copies the checkout to ~/.cartographer/app, symlinks ~/.local/bin/cartographer, and copies the skills to ~/.claude/skills/ (wrap, replay, complete, cartographer-setup).

- Touches ~/.claude/settings.json only with --auto, adding a SessionEnd hook that maps each session when it ends. Default is manual.

- Tells you if ~/.local/bin is not on your PATH, with the line to add.

- Windows: install.ps1 does the same with py or python, unpacks cartographer.zip, writes cartographer.cmd (PowerShell, cmd) and a shim for Git Bash (which Claude Code uses) into ~\.local\bin, and adds that folder to your user PATH. Hooks are registered as "python.exe" "…/bin/cartographer" hook claude-code, so they run without a Unix shell.

## Manual install

git clone https://github.com/situatedstrategies/cartographer && cd cartographer
./bin/cartographer install --agent claude-code # add --auto for hooks
cartographer config init # or: cartographer serve --open
cartographer doctor # what is installed, where, and what it found

### Update

Run the install line again. It replaces ~/.cartographer/app and the skills; your maps and config stay.

### Uninstall

rm -rf ~/.cartographer ~/.local/bin/cartographer ~/.claude/skills/{wrap,replay,complete,cartographer-setup}
# Windows (PowerShell): Remove-Item -Recurse ~\.cartographer, ~\.local\bin\cartographer*, ~\.claude\skills\wrap, ~\.claude\skills\replay, ~\.claude\skills\complete, ~\.claude\skills\cartographer-setup
# and, if you used --auto, remove the cartographer SessionEnd hook from ~/.claude/settings.json
Everything lives under ~/.cartographer (or $CARTOGRAPHER_HOME): config, one JSON map per session, appraisals, rendered replays. Raw transcripts are never copied there. Secrets are redacted before anything is written.

# In Claude Code · Cartographer
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/claude-code
Description: The four Cartographer commands inside Claude Code: /wrap, /replay, /complete, /cartographer-setup, and what a session looks like.

/wrap
At the end of a session. Cartographer digests the transcript into a timeline with a reading of every prompt, writes a brief tuned to your profile and the languages you used, and Claude writes the map: chapters, then moves (what you did, what happened, what it meant, how you responded), each citing its evidence. Then it files the map under the git repo you were in and renders the replay.
/wrap myproject names the project · /wrap --session <id> maps an older session · --force redoes one

/replay
The story of every wrapped session of a project, across branches, told one move at a time, with the playbook underneath: coaching, prompts worth reusing, how you build, where time went. /replay myproject, or just /replay to pick.

/complete
When a version is done. Claude asks what "done" meant, in your words, if you never declared it, then the result (shipped, partial, abandoned) and what actually happened. Then it writes the appraisal: what got you there, what cost you and how many minutes, what was carried into the result and what it will cost later, how you prompted and what it did. Every item cites session and move ids; praise words are rejected.

/cartographer-setup
Change your profile in conversation, switch manual and automatic wrapping, or backfill maps of old sessions. /cartographer-setup backfill lists past sessions and maps the ones you pick.

## What a session looks like

- Before you start (optional, recommended): cartographer goal "what done means for this version" in the repo. This is the yardstick every map is judged against.

- Build as usual. Prompts, corrections, dead ends, fixes. Cartographer is not running.

- /wrap at the end. Claude reads the brief, writes the map, saves it, and gives you the trailer: one line on what happened, three to five beats, one observation about how you build, coaching if you turned it on, and the replay path.

- Repeat across sessions. Each one lands in the same project; the replay stitches them into one story.

- /complete when the version ships. The honest reading of the whole build against what you wanted.

Codex and Cursor: coming soon. We're checking them against real session history before calling them supported.

# Commands · Cartographer
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/commands
Description: The complete Cartographer command reference: every command, its options, what it does and when to reach for it. Map a session, replay a project, declare a goal, judge a finished build.

## At a glance

Fourteen commands in four groups: looking at what you have, mapping a session, judging a version, and keeping the install healthy. Each one links to its full entry below.

| Command | | What it does |

| cartographer serve --open | | The dashboard in your browser, this machine only: profile, recent sessions with a Map this session button, projects, maps, outcomes and completion. |

| cartographer open [project] | | Open a replay directly. Newest project if you name none. |

| cartographer sessions --all | | Every session found for every installed agent. ✓ means already mapped. |

| cartographer projects | | Every project with its sessions, versions, declared outcomes and appraisals. |

| cartographer wrap [--session id] [--force] [--run] | | Write the brief for a session. --run also maps it with the agent's headless CLI, no human in the loop. |

| cartographer save file.json [--check] | | Validate, redact, file and render a map or an appraisal. --check only validates. This is what Claude runs at the end of /wrap. |

| cartographer backfill --cwd repo [--run] | | Briefs (or, with --run, maps) for every past session of a repo. Retrospective maps. |

| cartographer sweep [--dry] | | Map every session that has gone quiet and isn't mapped yet. For agents with no session-end event; run it on a schedule. |

| cartographer render --project name [--open] | | Rebuild a replay page. Also takes map and appraisal files directly. |

| cartographer goal "…" | | Declare what done means for the current version of the repo you are in. The source of truth for every map and the appraisal. |

| cartographer complete --result shipped|partial|abandoned --actual "…" | | Close the version and write the appraisal brief. --run appraises headlessly. |

| cartographer config show | set key value | init | | Your profile and settings, in the terminal. init is the wizard. |

| cartographer install --agent claude-code [--auto] | | What the installer runs. Rerun after updating. Codex and Cursor coming soon. |

| cartographer doctor | | Version, home folder, mode, which agents were found and how many sessions, headless runners. |

Windows: the same commands work in PowerShell, cmd and Git Bash. If cartographer is not found, open a new terminal so the PATH change takes effect.

## Looking at what you have

Four commands that change nothing. They show you the projects, sessions and maps Cartographer already knows about, in a browser or in the terminal.

### cartographer serve

cartographer serve --open{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Opens the dashboard: your profile, recent sessions with a Map this session button, projects, maps, outcomes and completion. It binds to 127.0.0.1 and refuses requests from anywhere else, so nothing is reachable from the network. Every button that changes something carries a per-run token, so a page open in another tab cannot trigger it.

- --open opens your browser on the dashboard as soon as it is up.

When to use it. When you want to see what has been mapped, pick a session to map by hand, or read a replay without remembering a project name. If you would rather click than type, this is the only command you need to learn.

### cartographer open

cartographer open [project]{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Renders and opens the replay for a project without going through the dashboard. Name no project and it opens the newest one.

- [project] is optional; the newest project is the default.

When to use it. The quickest route from a terminal to the story of a build. Pair it with projects when you have forgotten what a project is called.

### cartographer sessions

cartographer sessions --all{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Lists the sessions Cartographer can see. A tick marks the ones already mapped, so you can see at a glance what is still unmapped. Each line carries the session id you would pass to wrap.

- --all lists every agent's sessions, not only the current repo's.

When to use it. Before a backfill, or when you want to map one specific older session and need its id.

### cartographer projects

cartographer projects{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Lists everything Cartographer knows: each project, its sessions, its declared versions and goals, and the appraisals that closed them. It takes no options.

When to use it. An inventory, when you want to see the shape of the work across repos, or to check which versions still have no appraisal.

## Mapping a session

A map is written in two steps. Cartographer digests the transcript into a brief, and the agent that was in the session follows the brief to write the map. These five commands cover the brief, the filing, the catch-up for old sessions, and the rebuild of a replay.

### cartographer wrap

cartographer wrap [--session id] [--force] [--run]{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Digests a session's transcript into a timeline with a reading of every prompt, then writes the brief the agent uses to write the map. This is what the /wrap command in Claude Code runs before Claude does the writing. With no options it takes the latest session of the repo you are in.

- --session id wraps an older session instead of the latest one. Get the id from sessions.

- --force redoes a session that already has a brief.

- --run also maps it with the agent's headless CLI, with no human in the loop.

When to use it. At the end of a session, or from a script that maps sessions automatically. If you installed with --auto, Claude Code runs it for you when a session ends.

### cartographer save

cartographer save file.json [--check]{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Takes a map or appraisal file the agent has written, validates it against the rules, redacts secrets, files it under the project, and renders the replay. This is what Claude runs at the end of /wrap. The rules are the ones described on the How it works page: every move must cite the timeline items it rests on, "what it meant" has to name a technical implication, and praise words are rejected.

- --check only validates, and writes nothing. Useful when you are editing a map by hand and want to know whether it would be accepted.

When to use it. You rarely run it yourself. It is the last step of every wrap and every completion.

### cartographer backfill

cartographer backfill --cwd repo [--run]{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Prepares a brief for every session Claude Code still has on disk for a repo, so sessions from before you installed Cartographer can be mapped. This is what /cartographer-setup backfill runs.

- --cwd repo points at the repository whose sessions you want.

- --run maps them headlessly instead of only writing briefs.

When to use it. Once, after installing, to bring the history in. Retrospective maps read a little flatter than live ones, because nobody was there to be corrected.

### cartographer sweep

cartographer sweep [--dry]{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Finds sessions that have stopped and have no map, and maps them. It exists for agents that have no session-end event, and it is meant to be run on a schedule.

- --dry lists what would be mapped without mapping anything.

When to use it. From a scheduled job, when you want everything mapped without remembering to wrap. Run it with --dry first to see what it would pick up.

### cartographer render

cartographer render --project name [--open]{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Regenerates the replay for a project from its filed maps. It also accepts map and appraisal files directly, for rendering one on its own.

- --project name names the project to render.

- --open opens the result in your browser.

When to use it. After an update, or when a replay looks stale. open renders before it opens, so you only need this one when you want the file without the browser.

## Judging a version

Session maps are provisional. The outcome you wanted is only known when a version is done, so the verdict lives in these two commands: one to say what done means, one to say what actually happened.

### cartographer goal

cartographer goal "what done means"{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Records, in your words, what the current version of the repo is supposed to achieve. It is the source of truth for every map and for the appraisal: every session map is judged against it, and complete reads the result back against it.

- Takes one quoted sentence. Run it in the repo the version belongs to.

When to use it. Before you start a version, ideally. It is optional, and /complete will ask for it later if you never declared one. A goal written before the work is a better yardstick than one written after, because it has not yet been bent to fit the result.

### cartographer complete

cartographer complete --result shipped|partial|abandoned --actual "…"{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Marks a version as done, with the result and what actually happened, and writes the brief for the appraisal: what got you there, what it cost, what was carried into the result, how you prompted. Every appraisal item cites session and move ids, and praise words are rejected on save.

- --result is one of shipped, partial or abandoned.

- --actual is what actually happened, in your words.

- --run writes the appraisal headlessly instead of handing the brief to the agent in conversation.

When to use it. When a version ships, or when you abandon it. The verdict on the whole build lives here, because a session cannot judge itself. An abandoned version is worth completing too; the appraisal of a dead end is often the most useful one you get.

## Setup and health

Three commands for the install itself: the profile that shapes how maps are written, the registration with your agent, and the check to run when something is off.

### cartographer config

cartographer config show | set key value | init{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Shows or changes your profile and settings. The profile shapes every brief: whether moves are written in your words or in code terms, coaching on or off, which languages Cartographer knows you use. Settings live in ~/.cartographer and never leave your machine.

- show prints the current settings.

- set key value changes one.

- init runs the setup wizard again.

When to use it. When you want to change how maps are written without opening a conversation. /cartographer-setup does the same thing from inside Claude Code, and the dashboard has a form for it.

### cartographer install

cartographer install --agent claude-code [--auto]{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Registers Cartographer's commands with an agent. The one-line installer on the Install page runs this for you; rerun it after updating so the commands stay current.

- --agent claude-code is the only agent today. Codex and Cursor are coming soon.

- --auto turns on automatic wrapping at the end of every session.

When to use it. After the install line, and again after an update. Switching between manual and automatic wrapping later is a config change, not a reinstall.

### cartographer doctor

cartographer doctor{this.textContent='Copied';setTimeout(()=>this.textContent='Copy',1500)})">Copy

Prints what Cartographer can see: its version, the home folder, whether wrapping is manual or automatic, which agents were found and how many sessions each has, and which headless runners are available. It takes no options and changes nothing.

When to use it. First thing to run when something does not work, and the output to paste when you write to support@codecartographer.dev.

# How it works · Cartographer
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/how-it-works
Description: How Cartographer reads session history, reads every prompt, briefs the agent and judges the build against a yardstick.

Reads what already exists
Claude Code keeps one file per session. An adapter turns it into a plain stream of events: prompts, replies, tools, errors, branch changes. No capture, no plugin in the loop, no cloud.

Reads every prompt
What act it performs (build, fix, repair, accept, ask), what it anchors to (files, symbols, errors, pasted code), how it is said (imperative, question, hedged, delegated). A turn that starts with "no, I meant…" marks the previous move as having gone wrong for you, even if the code ran.

Hands the agent a brief
Facts, your profile, what Cartographer knows about the languages you used, the reading of each prompt, the rules, the timeline. The agent that was in the session writes the map. Any agent can follow the same brief.

Judges against a yardstick
Session maps are provisional. The outcome you wanted is only known when a version is done, so /complete is where the verdict lives. Every move and every appraisal item must cite its evidence in the record; praise words are rejected on save.

## The shape of a map

A session map is a list of moves. Each move has the same five parts, in your words or in code terms depending on your profile.

| Part | | Answers |

| you | | What you did: the prompt, the correction, the decision, the pause. |

| happened | | What the agent did with it and what the tools returned. |

| consequence | | What that meant technically: the file that changed shape, the test that now passes, the assumption that got baked in. |

| outcome | | worked · partly · broke · wrong way · opened a question. Judged from the record, not from tone. |

| response | | How you responded next, and whether it repaired, accepted or moved on. |

Moves are grouped into chapters. Marks call out decisions, questions, dead ends, fixes, artifacts, pivots and insights. The replay plays them in order; the appraisal reads them against the yardstick.

# Questions · Cartographer
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/questions
Description: Privacy, Windows, .pkg, updating, old sessions, and what honest means mechanically.

Does anything leave my machine?No. Maps, config and replays live in ~/.cartographer. The dashboard binds to 127.0.0.1 and refuses requests from anywhere else. The only network call is the installer downloading Cartographer. Team sharing, when it comes, will be a choice you make, not a default.

Is there a Mac installer (.pkg)?Not yet. A signed and notarised package is on the list. The one-line installer does the same thing on Mac and Linux without needing Apple's signing, and it is what we test.

Windows?Yes, natively: the PowerShell line on the Install page. It needs Python 3.9+ (winget install Python.Python.3.12) and Claude Code, which brings Git Bash with it. The Windows path is new and has had less real-world use than Mac and Linux; if anything breaks, support@codecartographer.dev with the output of the installer is enough to fix it. WSL works as well.

Can I map sessions from before I installed it?Yes. /cartographer-setup backfill or cartographer backfill --cwd <repo> prepares a brief for every past session Claude Code still has on disk.

What does "honest" mean here, mechanically?Three enforced rules. Every move lists the timeline items it rests on. "What it meant" has to name the technical implication, not an adjective. Saving rejects praise words in the map and the appraisal. And the verdict waits for completion, because a session cannot judge itself.

How do I update?Run the install line again. It replaces ~/.cartographer/app and the skills; your maps and config stay.

Which agents?Claude Code, today. Codex and Cursor are coming soon. We're checking them against real session history before calling them supported.

Something broke. Where do I write?support@codecartographer.dev with what you typed and what came back. Maps you'd like to show us, or thoughts on the maps you got: mapit@codecartographer.dev.

# How to read a Claude Code session log: the JSONL files explained
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/guides/reading-claude-code-session-logs
Description: Where Claude Code keeps session history, what each line of the JSONL file holds, how to read one by hand, and what a transcript cannot tell you on its own.

## What is in the file

Claude Code stores every session as a JSONL file, one JSON object per line, under ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-project-path>/<session-id>.jsonl. The project folder is your working directory path with non-alphanumeric characters replaced by hyphens.1 Each line is one event: a user turn, an assistant reply, a tool call, a tool result, or a system event. The file is append-only; new events are new lines.2

Each event carries top-level fields such as type, uuid, parentUuid, timestamp, sessionId, cwd, gitBranch and version. Inside message.content are content blocks: text, thinking, tool_use with an id, a name and its input, and tool_result referencing the tool_use_id it answers.2 That is enough structure to rebuild the whole session in order: which prompt led to which tool call, what came back, and what the agent said next.

## Reading it by hand

Find the folder for your project, sort by modification time, and open the newest file. Filter lines by type to see only user turns, or only tool results. The parentUuid chain is the conversation thread; the gitBranch field tells you where you were when each turn happened. A short script that prints timestamp, type and the first line of each text block gives you a readable transcript in a minute.

There are also community tools that render transcripts as pages, such as Simon Willison's claude-code-transcripts.3 They answer the question "what was said", which is the right first question.

## What a transcript does not tell you

A transcript is the record of what happened, in order. It does not say which prompt was the one that went wrong, which correction repaired it, where the time went, or whether the build ended up where you said it should. Those are readings of the record, and they are the part that takes the work.

That is the part Cartographer does. It reads the same file through an adapter that turns it into a plain stream of events, reads every prompt for what act it performs and what it anchors to, and hands the agent that was in the session a brief. The agent writes the map: chapters, then moves, each with what you did, what happened, what it meant, how it turned out and how you responded, each citing the timeline it rests on. How it works has the detail, and the demo replay shows a real build read this way.

## Questions

Where does Claude Code keep session history?Under your home folder, in ~/.claude/projects/, one folder per project, one JSONL file per session. The folder name is the project path with non-alphanumeric characters replaced by hyphens.

Can I read the file without a tool?Yes. It is plain text, one JSON object per line. Any editor opens it, and a line of jq or a few lines of Python turn it into something readable.

Does Cartographer copy my transcripts?No. It reads them where they are and writes maps, briefs and replays under ~/.cartographer. Raw transcripts are never copied there, and secrets are redacted before anything is written.

Does any of this leave my machine?Not through Cartographer. The dashboard binds to 127.0.0.1, and the only network call the tool makes is the installer downloading it.

## Sources

- Claude Code documentation. Explore the .claude directory.

- Claude Code documentation. Manage sessions.

- Simon Willison. claude-code-transcripts, on GitHub.

# Cartographer vs git history vs a chat summary: what each records
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/compare
Description: Git records what changed. A chat summary records what the agent remembers. A Cartographer map records how the build went, move by move, with evidence.

| | | Git history | | A chat summary | | A Cartographer map |

| Records | | What changed: commits, diffs, branches | | What the agent remembers, in prose | | Every move: what you did, what happened, what it meant, the outcome, your response |

| Evidence | | The diff itself | | None required | | Each move lists the timeline items it rests on; saving rejects a move without them |

| Dead ends | | Invisible unless committed | | Usually left out | | Kept, marked, and read for what they cost |

| Your prompts | | Not recorded | | Paraphrased | | Read one by one: the act, the anchor, how it was said, and where a correction marks the previous move as wrong for you |

| Praise | | Not applicable | | Common | | Rejected on save, in the map and in the appraisal |

| The verdict | | Whether it merged | | Whatever the summary says | | Waits for /complete, judged against the goal you declared, because a session cannot judge itself |

| Where it lives | | The repo | | The chat | | ~/.cartographer on your machine, as JSON maps and rendered replays |

## The short version

Git is the record of the result. A chat summary is the agent's recollection of the process. A map is the process, read from the record, under rules. Use all three; they do not compete.

If you want to see what the third one looks like on a real build, the demo replay is one. How it works explains the five parts of a move and the yardstick the appraisal reads them against.

## Questions

Does Cartographer replace git?No. Git records what changed and Cartographer records how you got there. They answer different questions about the same work.

Why not just ask the agent to summarise the session?You can, and it will. A summary is prose with no rules: it can praise, skip the dead ends, and cite nothing. A map has five fixed parts per move, cites the timeline it rests on, and rejects praise words on save. The difference shows up the third time you read one.

Is the map written by a different model?It is written by the agent that was in the session, following a brief. That is why it knows what you meant. The rules are enforced by Cartographer when the map is saved, not by the model's good intentions.

# About · Cartographer
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/about
Description: Who makes Cartographer, why it exists, what it does and does not do, and how to reach the people behind it.

## What Cartographer is

Cartographer is an open source command line tool, released under the MIT licence, that reads the session history your coding agent already keeps and tells it back to you as a story: what you asked for, what the agent did, what that meant technically, and how you responded. It files each map under the git repository it belongs to, replays the whole build when a project is done, and judges the build against the goal you declared before you started.

It works with Claude Code today. Codex and Cursor support is coming once we have checked it against real session history. Cartographer is plain Python with no dependencies, it runs on your machine only, and the only network call it ever makes is the installer downloading the tool. Nothing about your sessions leaves your computer. That is a design decision, not a current limitation, and it is explained in detail on the Privacy page.

## Why it exists

Git records what changed. It does not record how you got there: the prompt that sent the agent in circles for forty minutes, the correction that finally landed, the moment you stopped reading and started trusting. A few weeks into a build those moments are gone, and all that is left is the diff.

The transcript has all of it. Every prompt, every reply, every tool call and error is sitting in a file on your disk. It is just unreadable at the length it comes in. Cartographer's job is to make that record legible without flattering anyone: every claim in a map has to cite the moment in the transcript it came from, "what it meant" has to name a technical consequence rather than an adjective, and the tool rejects praise words on save. The verdict on a version waits until the version is done, because a session cannot judge itself.

The method behind that comes from a particular way of studying work. The person behind Situated Strategies is a software implementation specialist by day and a doctoral researcher in ethnomethodology and conversation analysis, the study of how people actually get things done together, turn by turn, in the record of what they said and did. Cartographer applies that habit of reading to the turns between a person and an agent. The questions it asks of a transcript are the same ones that discipline asks of any recorded interaction: what did this turn do, what did the next turn make of it, and where did the work go off course and get repaired?

## Who makes it

Cartographer is made by Situated Strategies LLC, a small company in the United States. The company builds practical tools and products around one idea: that the best guide to how something should work is a close look at how people actually use it. Cartographer is its first developer tool.

The source is public at github.com/situatedstrategies/cartographer. Issues, pull requests and forks are welcome. The tool is free, and it will stay free; if it has been useful to you, there is a Ko-fi page for people who want to support the work.

## What we will not do

We will not send your session history anywhere. We will not add telemetry to the tool. We will not describe what any coding agent does internally beyond what its vendor documents, and when we cite research or documentation on this site, the citation links to the source and says no more than the source does. When team sharing arrives it will be something you turn on, not a default.

## Reaching us

Something broke, or a question about the tool: support@codecartographer.dev, ideally with the output of cartographer doctor. A map you would like to show us, or thoughts on the maps you got: mapit@codecartographer.dev. Both addresses are read by a person.

This page was last updated October 8th 2026.

← QuestionsPrivacy →

# Privacy · Cartographer
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/privacy
Description: What the Cartographer tool and the codecartographer.dev site do with your data: the tool sends nothing, the site sets no cookies of its own, and the third parties it loads are listed here by name.

## The Cartographer tool

Cartographer runs entirely on your machine. Maps, configuration and replays are stored in a folder called ~/.cartographer in your home directory. The local dashboard binds to 127.0.0.1 and refuses requests from any other address, so it is not reachable from your network. The tool contains no analytics, no crash reporting and no telemetry of any kind.

The only network call the tool ever makes is the installer downloading Cartographer itself from this site. After that, nothing it reads and nothing it writes leaves your computer. Your session transcripts, the maps built from them, your profile and your declared goals stay with you. We cannot see them, and we have no way to ask for them.

Before a map is filed, the save command redacts secrets it recognises, such as keys and tokens that appear in a transcript. This is a courtesy for the day you choose to share a map with someone, not a substitute for your own review: the redaction is pattern based and can miss things.

## The website

codecartographer.dev is a static site served by Cloudflare. The pages themselves set no cookies and carry no analytics script of their own. We do not run a newsletter, there are no accounts, and there is no form that stores what you type.

Like any web host, Cloudflare processes the technical details of each request, such as your IP address and browser type, to deliver the page and to protect the site from abuse. That processing is governed by Cloudflare's privacy policy.

### Third parties the pages load

When a page loads it asks the following services for a file, which means each of them receives the technical details of that request, including your IP address. Browser extensions that block third party requests will stop all of them, and the site still works without any of them.

- Google AdSense. The pages carry Google's advertising script. Google, as a third party vendor, uses cookies to serve ads based on your prior visits to this website or other websites. Google's use of advertising cookies enables it and its partners to serve ads to you based on your visit to this site and other sites on the Internet. You can opt out of personalised advertising at Google's ads settings. How Google uses data when you use a site that carries its services is explained at policies.google.com/technologies/partner-sites.

- Google Fonts. The typefaces are loaded from fonts.googleapis.com and fonts.gstatic.com. Google's handling of those requests is covered by the same page linked above.

- Ko-fi. The floating support button is a script loaded from storage.ko-fi.com. Nothing happens unless you click it; if you do, you are dealing with Ko-fi under Ko-fi's own terms and privacy policy.

- PeerPush. The badge in the footer is an image loaded from peerpush.com.

The demo replay on this site is Cartographer's own map of the sessions that built Cartographer, with secrets redacted. It is a file in the public repository, not a live view of anything.

## Email

Mail sent to support@codecartographer.dev or mapit@codecartographer.dev is received by Cloudflare Email Routing, tagged by the mailbox it was addressed to, and forwarded to an inbox read by a person at Situated Strategies. We keep your message for as long as it takes to deal with it and for our own records of what was reported. We do not add your address to any list and we do not share it. If you send us a map, we treat it as private unless you tell us otherwise in the same message.

## Your choices and your rights

You can read this site with third party requests blocked and lose nothing. You can delete everything the tool has ever stored by removing the ~/.cartographer folder. If you have written to us and want your message deleted, say so at support@codecartographer.dev and we will delete it. Residents of jurisdictions with data protection laws, including the European Union, the United Kingdom and California, have rights of access, correction and deletion over any personal data we hold, which in practice is limited to the email you chose to send us.

This site is not directed at children under the age of 13, and we do not knowingly collect personal information from them.

## Changes

If this policy changes, the new version is published here with a new date. Material changes, such as adding an analytics service, will be called out on this page for at least thirty days.

This policy is published by Situated Strategies LLC and was last updated October 8th 2026.

# Terms · Cartographer
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/terms
Description: The terms for using the Cartographer tool, which is MIT licensed, and the codecartographer.dev website, in plain language.

## The tool

Cartographer is released under the MIT licence. In short: you may use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell copies of it, provided the copyright notice and the licence text travel with it. The full licence is in the repository, and it is the text that governs; this paragraph is a summary.

The MIT licence also says, in capital letters, that the software is provided as is, without warranty of any kind, and that the authors are not liable for any claim or damages arising from its use. That is as true of Cartographer as of any other MIT licensed tool. Maps and appraisals are generated from your transcripts by the coding agent you already use, following a brief Cartographer writes; they can be wrong, and the verdict they give is a reading of the record, not a guarantee about your code.

## The installer

The one-line installers on the Install page download Cartographer from this site and place it in your home directory. They are short scripts, and you are welcome to read them before running them: install.sh and install.ps1. Running a script you fetched from the internet is your decision, and the warranty disclaimer above applies to the installer as much as to the tool.

## The website

The text, design and images on codecartographer.dev are copyright Situated Strategies LLC unless another source is named. Quoting from the site with a link back is fine. Republishing whole pages is not. The pages of the site are in the same public repository as the tool and carry the same MIT licence. The Cartographer name and logo are not part of that grant and may not be used in a way that suggests we made or endorsed something we did not.

Blog posts on this site cite their sources. The cited material belongs to its authors and publishers, and a citation is not a claim of endorsement by them. Where this site describes another company's product, it does so from that company's own documentation, linked.

The site is offered as is. We try to keep it accurate and online, and we fix errors when they are pointed out, but we make no promise that it is complete, current or uninterrupted.

## Advertising and support

The site carries advertising served by Google AdSense, which is how a free tool pays for its hosting. Ads are selected by Google, not by us, and an ad's presence on a page is not a recommendation. The Ko-fi button is a way to support the work voluntarily; nothing on the site or in the tool is gated behind it.

## Contact and changes

Questions about these terms go to support@codecartographer.dev. If the terms change, the new version is published here with a new date. These terms are governed by the laws of the United States and of the state in which Situated Strategies LLC is organised.

These terms are published by Situated Strategies LLC and were last updated October 8th 2026.

# What the research says about reviewing code you didn't write
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/blog/reviewing-code-you-did-not-write
Description: Two studies of code review put understanding the change first. Here's what they found, and what it means when you didn't write the code.

Most of us picture code review as hunting. You scan a diff, you spot the off-by-one, you flag it. The research paints a different picture, and it's worth knowing before you sit down to read the next change you didn't write.

## Review isn't mostly about bugs

In 2013, Alberto Bacchelli and Christian Bird studied code review at Microsoft. They observed, interviewed and surveyed developers and managers, and they classified hundreds of review comments across diverse teams. Their finding was that finding defects remains the main motivation for review, but reviews are less about defects than expected.1 People got other things out of it too: knowledge transfer, team awareness, and alternative solutions to the problem at hand.1

The part that matters most for us is what they named as the center of the activity. In their words, code and change understanding is the key aspect of code reviewing, and developers used mechanisms to get it that current tools don't meet.1

## What reviewers actually do

A more recent study looks at the how. Pavlína Wurzel Gonçalves and colleagues, writing for the 2025 International Conference on Program Comprehension, observed and interviewed ten experienced reviewers as they worked through 25 reviews, and read what they saw through code comprehension theory.2

They report that reviewers work opportunistically. The strategies they describe usually start with a phase of building context. Only then does the reviewer move into inspecting the code, which involves reading it, testing it, and managing discussion.2

Notice the order. Context comes first, and reading the lines comes second.

## What this means when you didn't write it

Neither study was about coding agents, and we won't pretend otherwise. They looked at people reviewing changes made by other people. What follows is our own reading, not a finding.

If understanding is the hard part of review, then the least understood changes are the riskiest ones to wave through. A change you didn't write, made for reasons you weren't in the room for, starts you at zero. That's true of a colleague's pull request. We'd argue it's just as true of code that arrived while you were typing prompts and watching a terminal scroll.

So the studies suggest a few habits that cost very little:

- Build context before you read the diff. What was this change meant to do, and why now?

- Treat "I can't explain this yet" as a real review result, not a delay.

- Test it, don't just read it. Testing is part of how experienced reviewers inspect code in the second study.

- Keep notes on the reasons behind the change, so you aren't rebuilding them from memory later.

That last one is where a session record helps. Cartographer reads the session history your coding agent already keeps and turns it into a map of how a project was built: what you asked, what happened, and how you responded. It reads what's already on your machine, with no cloud. When you come back to a change weeks later, the context you'd have to rebuild is already written down.

## Why this is a kindness to your future self

There's a quieter point here. Understanding is work, and work gets skipped when we're tired or when a change looks tidy. A clean diff feels like a finished thought. It isn't evidence that anyone understood it, least of all you.

We've all approved something because the tests passed and the summary sounded sure of itself. Sometimes that's fine. But passing tests tell you the code does what the tests ask, not that you know what you've agreed to carry. When something breaks months later, the person who has to untangle it is you, and you'll be reading it cold.

None of this needs a new tool or a long checklist. It needs a pause long enough to say, in your own words, what the change does and why it exists. If you can't, you've learned something useful, and it cost you a minute instead of a week.

## A small shift in the question

"Is this correct?" is a fine question. But the research suggests it comes second. First comes "do I understand what this change is trying to do?" If the answer is no, the review hasn't really started, and that's worth knowing before you hit merge.

## Sources

- Alberto Bacchelli and Christian Bird. Expectations, Outcomes, and Challenges of Modern Code Review. 35th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE), 2013.

- Pavlína Wurzel Gonçalves, Pooja Rani, Margaret-Anne Storey, Diomidis Spinellis and Alberto Bacchelli. Code Review Comprehension: Reviewing Strategies Seen Through Code Comprehension Theories. International Conference on Program Comprehension (ICPC), 2025. arXiv:2503.21455.

Questions, or a topic you'd like us to dig into next? Reach out any time: support@codecartographer.dev. We read everything.

# Why a correction is the most informative prompt in a session
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/blog/why-corrections-are-the-most-informative-prompt
Description: A correction shows the gap between what you asked and what you meant. Here's what repair research and one vendor's docs say about reading it.

Every session has a few prompts that do more work than the rest. They aren't the long ones or the clever ones. They're the short, slightly deflated ones: "No, I meant the other file." "Not that. Keep the old behavior." "Why did you rewrite the tests?"

A correction is the moment a conversation stops and checks itself. That makes it unusually rich in information, and it's worth knowing why.

## A correction is a measurement of a gap

A first prompt is a guess about how to say what you want. The reply is a test of that guess. When the reply is right, you learn little, because the words did their job. When it's wrong, you learn something specific: the sentence you wrote and the thing you meant weren't the same.

The correction is where that gap gets written down. It usually names what was missing. A constraint you assumed was obvious. A file you thought was implied. A word that meant one thing to you and another to the reader. No other prompt in the session says so much about what you hadn't said.

## Conversation researchers have studied this for decades

People fix misunderstandings all the time when they talk, and there's a body of work on how. In 1977, Schegloff, Jefferson and Sacks published a paper on the preference for self-correction in the organization of repair in conversation.1 Their subject was the machinery speakers use to deal with recurring problems in speaking, hearing and understanding.1

Two points from that tradition carry over well. First, repair is a normal part of talk, not a sign that something has gone badly wrong. Second, the person who spots the trouble and the person who caused it aren't always the same, and who fixes what matters. In that paper, the authors describe a preference for self-correction over correction by someone else.1

Later work found that this isn't a quirk of one language. A survey of repair requests in twenty-one languages reports that speakers of all the spoken languages sampled have a monosyllabic "huh?"-type interjection that is strikingly similar across languages.2 Our reading: "huh?" flags that something went wrong without saying what, and people everywhere seem to want a cheap way to say "that didn't land."

None of this research is about coding agents, and we won't pretend it is. Reading it across is our own interpretation. But the shape fits. In a session, you are the one who knows what you meant. The reply is the one that missed. Your correction is you repairing a misunderstanding that began in your own wording.

## What the vendor's own guidance says

Anthropic's documentation for Claude Code treats correction as a routine part of the work. Its best-practices page advises you to correct Claude as soon as you notice it going off track, and says that correcting quickly generally produces better solutions faster.3

The same page also marks a limit. It says that if you've corrected Claude more than twice on the same issue in one session, the context is cluttered with failed approaches, and it suggests clearing the session and starting fresh with a more specific prompt that incorporates what you learned.3 It lists "correcting over and over" among the common failure patterns.3

Read that as a point about information. One correction tells you what was missing. A third correction on the same issue tells you the repair isn't working, and the thing to change is the prompt itself.

## How to read your own corrections

If a correction is a measurement of a gap, you can learn from the measurements. A few questions help:

- What did the correction add that the first prompt lacked? A constraint, a scope, a name, a preference?

- Could you have known to say it up front? If yes, that's a reusable habit. If no, it was just discovery.

- Did the correction fix things, or did you need another one? A string of them on one issue is a sign to restart.

- Did you correct the reply, or your own earlier prompt? Both happen, and they teach different things.

Over many sessions, the same gaps tend to show up. Maybe you always forget to say which tests to leave alone. Maybe you name things loosely. Those patterns are hard to see from inside a single session and easy to see in a pile of them.

## Where a record helps

Cartographer reads the session history your coding agent already keeps and turns it into a map of how a project was built. Its maps note what you did, including the prompt, the correction and the decision, and how you responded next: whether you repaired, accepted or moved on. It reads what's already on your machine, with no cloud. If you want to look back at your corrections as a set, that's what the record is for.

## A small habit

Next time you type a correction, pause for a second before sending it. Ask what the first prompt would have needed to say for the correction not to exist. You don't have to act on the answer. Just notice it. Over time, the corrections you write will tell you more about how you ask than about what the agent did.

## Sources

- Schegloff, Jefferson and Sacks. The Preference for Self-Correction in the Organization of Repair in Conversation. Language, vol. 53, no. 2, 1977, pp. 361-382.

- Enfield, Dingemanse and colleagues. Chapter 12, Huh? What? - A first survey in 21 languages. OAPEN library.

- Anthropic. Best practices for Claude Code. Claude Code documentation, section "Course-correct early and often" and "Avoid common failure patterns".

Questions, or a topic you'd like us to dig into next? Reach out any time: mapit@codecartographer.dev. We read everything.

# Declaring done before you start: goals as a yardstick
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/blog/declaring-done-before-you-start
Description: Goal-setting research and the agile 'definition of done' agree: say what finished looks like first. Here's why that helps when an agent writes the code.

You ask for a feature. The agent works, the tests go green, the summary says it's finished. Is it? That depends on a question you may never have answered: finished compared to what?

If the answer only forms after the work is on your screen, you end up judging the result by how it feels. A tidy diff feels done. A confident summary feels done. Neither is a yardstick. This post is about setting the yardstick first.

## What goal research found

Edwin Locke and Gary Latham spent decades studying how goals shape work. In a 2002 review of 35 years of their research, they report that specific, difficult goals consistently led to higher performance than urging people to do their best.1 "Do your best" sounds encouraging. It's also a goal nobody can fail, because it never says what success is.

The same review is careful about conditions. The advantage holds when people get feedback about their progress, are committed to the goal, and have the ability and knowledge to do the task.1 A goal does two jobs here. It directs effort, and it gives you something to measure against as you go.

That research is about people doing work, mostly people doing their own. It isn't about coding agents, and we won't claim it is. What follows is our reading of it, not a finding.

## What agile teams call it

Software teams reached for the same idea under a different name. In Scrum, the Definition of Done is a written statement of what it takes for work to count as complete. Scrum.org's write-up says that work that fails the Definition of Done isn't released or shown at the Sprint Review and goes back to the Product Backlog.2

Notice what it does for a team. Nobody has to argue, afterwards, about whether something is finished. The argument happened earlier, when it was cheap.

## Why it matters more with an agent

When you write the code yourself, you carry the goal in your head and adjust it as you go. When something else writes it, your head isn't in the loop in the same way. You see a result and have to decide what to make of it.

Without a stated finish line, three things tend to happen:

- The goal drifts. Each new prompt nudges it, and nobody notices the sum.

- "Done" becomes whatever the agent reports. Its summary becomes the yardstick, which makes it both the author and the judge.

- Extras slip in. Without edges, anything that works looks like progress.

None of that is anyone's fault. It's what happens when there's nothing to compare against.

## What a good yardstick looks like

It doesn't need to be long. A few lines before you start will do:

- The outcome, in terms someone could observe. "Users can reset their password by email," not "improve login."

- What would show it works. A test, a command you can run, a page you can open.

- What's out of scope. Naming the edges stops the slow creep.

- What you'd accept as good enough. Specific doesn't have to mean perfect.

Then comes the part people skip: compare the result against what you wrote, not against what you now remember wanting. Memory is generous to whatever got built.

You're also allowed to revise the yardstick. Plans change, and sometimes the build teaches you what you actually wanted. Just change it on purpose, in writing, rather than letting it slide.

## Where a session record helps

Cartographer reads the session history your coding agent already keeps and turns it into a map of how a project was built. Because the outcome you wanted is only known when a version is done, it treats session maps as provisional. You can declare what done means with cartographer goal, each wrap is judged against it, and /complete writes the closing reading. It all runs on your machine, with no cloud.

## A small habit to try

Before your next prompt, write one sentence that starts with "This is done when." If you can't finish it, that's useful news, and it arrived before any code did. If you can, you've given yourself something the summary can't talk you out of.

## Sources

- Edwin A. Locke and Gary P. Latham. Building a Practically Useful Theory of Goal Setting and Task Motivation: A 35-Year Odyssey. American Psychologist, 57(9), 705-717, 2002.

- Scrum.org. TL; DR: Definition of Done Theses. Scrum.org blog.

Questions, or a topic you'd like us to dig into next? Reach out any time: support@codecartographer.dev. We read everything.

# Reading your own dead ends
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/blog/reading-your-own-dead-ends
Description: Abandoned branches and discarded attempts aren't waste. What research on abandoned work and recorded rationale says, and how to read your own.

Open any repository you've worked in for a while and look at the branches. Some merged. Some are still sitting there, three weeks stale, named something hopeful. We all have a few of those, and we rarely open them again.

We'd like to make a case for opening them. Not out of nostalgia, and not to feel bad about unfinished work. A dead end holds something the finished code doesn't: a record of what you tried, and why it didn't hold.

## Abandoned work is common, and mostly silent

It helps to know how ordinary this is. Researchers studying open source have counted it. Khatoonabadi and colleagues built a dataset of 265,325 pull requests, including 4,450 abandoned ones, from ten popular and mature GitHub projects.1 That's a small share of the total, but it's far from zero, and these were well-run projects.

They also read through a random sample of 354 abandoned pull requests to ask why. Their abstract reports that the most common reasons for abandonment involve obstacles faced by contributors, followed by hurdles imposed by maintainers during the review process.1 On the question of what makes abandonment more likely, they link complex pull requests, novice contributors and lengthy reviews to a higher chance of abandonment.1

Notice what's missing from that list. Nobody abandons work because they were careless. They abandon it because it got hard, or slow, or tangled. That's exactly the kind of information a team would want back later, and it's exactly the kind that disappears when a branch gets deleted.

## The reasons are the valuable part

Software engineering has a name for the thing we lose. It's called rationale: the reasons behind a design, not just the design. Janet Burge, John Carroll, Raymond McCall and Ivan Mistrik wrote a whole book on it. Their starting point is that design decisions and the decision-making process behind them can best be documented as the rationale for the system, and they follow that idea through the software lifecycle, from the first decisions in a project to maintenance and reuse.2

Here's our own reading of that, and it's an inference rather than something the book says in these words. A discarded attempt is a piece of rationale in its purest form. It's a decision (we tried this) with an outcome (it didn't work) that nobody had to argue for afterward. Finished code shows you the path that survived. Dead ends show you the walls.

## What a dead end can tell you

When we go back through our own abandoned attempts, a few questions tend to be useful:

- What were we trying to do when we started down this path? The goal is often clearer in the first hour than the last.

- Where did it stop working? A specific error teaches more than a vague sense that it was "getting messy."

- Did we leave because the idea was wrong, or because the moment was? Those are different lessons.

- Would we make the same call again, knowing what we know now?

The third question matters most to us. Some ideas fail because they're bad. Others fail because we ran out of time, or got pulled into something urgent. If you can't tell which was which, you may end up avoiding a good idea for years, or retrying a bad one with fresh optimism.

## Why we don't do it

There's a human reason we skip this. Abandoned work feels like a small failure, and we'd rather move on. Memory helps us along by smoothing the story: we remember the version that shipped and forget the three that didn't.

There's a practical reason too. The evidence is scattered. A branch name tells you almost nothing. The commit history shows what you kept, not what you tried and reverted. The reasoning lived in your head, or in a chat, or in a terminal you've since closed.

If you build with a coding agent, some of that reasoning is written down already, because the session itself is a record of the attempt. Cartographer reads the session history your agent already keeps and turns it into a map of how a project was built, with turning points marked. It records which branch each session was on, and it all stays on your machine. That's a place to start when you want to see where a build changed course.

## A small habit

You don't need a process. Next time you abandon a branch, write two sentences before you walk away: what you were trying, and why you stopped. Put them in the branch description, a commit message, or a notes file. Future you will be reading cold, and two honest sentences are worth more than a clean history.

Dead ends aren't the opposite of progress. They're how the map gets its edges.

## Sources

- SayedHassan Khatoonabadi, Diego Elias Costa, Rabe Abdalkareem and Emad Shihab. On Wasted Contributions: Understanding the Dynamics of Contributor-Abandoned Pull Requests. arXiv:2110.15447.

- Janet E. Burge, John M. Carroll, Raymond McCall and Ivan Mistrik. Rationale-Based Software Engineering. Springer, 2008.

Questions, or a topic you'd like us to dig into next? Reach out any time: mapit@codecartographer.dev. We read everything.

# Praise is not evidence: appraising an agent's work honestly
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/blog/praise-is-not-evidence
Description: A confident summary or an 'all done' feels like proof. Two studies suggest why that's risky, and a few plain habits for appraising work honestly.

We know the feeling. The terminal goes quiet, a tidy summary scrolls past, and it ends with "all done." Something in us relaxes. We nod, maybe say thanks, and move on.

That relaxed feeling is worth a second look. It's a reaction to tone, and tone isn't evidence of anything. Here's what some research says about why we're so ready to accept automated output, and what we can do about it.

## Leaning on the machine is an old habit

Researchers have a name for it: automation bias, the tendency to over-rely on automation.1 A 2012 systematic review by Kate Goddard, Abdul Roudsari and Jeremy Wyatt looked at it across several research fields, with a focus on clinical decision support in healthcare. Of 13,821 papers retrieved, 74 met their inclusion criteria.1

One observation from that review stays with us. Although most research shows overall improved performance with these tools, there is often a failure to recognize the new errors the tools can introduce.1 The help is real, and so is the blind spot it creates. Both are true at once.

The review also found that how much people lean on automation isn't fixed. Factors such as cognitive style, task specific experience, trust and confidence all played a part, and so did workload, task complexity and time constraints.1 Notice that last group. Busy, hurried people lean harder. That describes most of us at the end of a long session.

## Feeling sure and being right are different things

A second study is closer to our own world. Neil Perry, Megha Srivastava, Deepak Kumar and Dan Boneh ran a user study of people writing code with and without an AI assistant. They found that participants with access to an AI assistant wrote significantly less secure code than those without.2 They also found that the assisted participants were more likely to believe they had written secure code.2

The authors suggest this means such tools may lead users to be overconfident about security flaws in their code.2 That's their reading, and it's worth keeping it that modest. The study was about security tasks and one particular assistant, not about every kind of work. It also noted something encouraging: participants who trusted the AI less and engaged more with their prompts wrote code with fewer vulnerabilities.2

Neither study tells us how any given coding agent behaves, and we won't claim they do. What they show is on the human side of the screen. We can feel secure about work that isn't. And when something automated is helping, we're prone to miss the errors it adds.

## Praise is a mood, not a measurement

So here's our own view, offered as a view and not as a finding. A summary that says "all done" is a statement about the work, written by the one who did it. Sometimes it's right. But it's still only a statement. It can't tell you whether the thing you meant is the thing you got.

When a person tells us "it's finished," we usually ask to see it. We should extend the same courtesy to a tool, and to ourselves when we're feeling pleased. A few habits help:

- Run it. Open the page, call the function, feed it the awkward input. Watching it work beats reading that it works.

- Compare it to what you asked for. Reread your original request, not the summary of it.

- Ask what would prove it wrong. If nothing could, you haven't tested anything yet.

- Look for what the summary skipped. The omissions are often where the trouble sits.

- Slow down when you're rushed. That's when leaning is strongest.

None of this is distrust. It's the ordinary habit of checking work before we sign for it, and it's kinder to our future selves than finding out in production.

## Where a record helps

There's one more piece. To compare the result with what you meant, you need to remember what you meant, and what happened along the way. Cartographer reads the session history your coding agent already keeps and tells each session back to you as a story: what you did, what happened, and how you responded. It reads what's already on your machine, with no cloud. It's a way to look at the build instead of only at its closing summary.

## A smaller kind of honesty

We think appraising work honestly is mostly a matter of keeping two questions apart. "Does this sound finished?" and "Is this what we meant?" feel alike in the moment. Only the second one is evidence. It takes a minute to ask, and it's usually the cheapest minute of the whole project.

## Sources

- Kate Goddard, Abdul Roudsari and Jeremy C. Wyatt. Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators. Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 19(1), 2012.

- Neil Perry, Megha Srivastava, Deepak Kumar and Dan Boneh. Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?. ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS), 2023. arXiv:2211.03622.

# Write the spec before you delegate, to an agent or a colleague
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/blog/write-the-spec-before-you-delegate
Description: Requirements research keeps finding incomplete requirements among the most critical problems. Here's what that means before you hand work off.

Delegating feels efficient. You describe the job in a sentence or two, someone else (or something else) takes it, and your afternoon is free. Then the result comes back and it isn't quite what you pictured. Nobody did anything wrong. The picture just never left your head.

## What practitioners report

Software engineers have studied this gap for a long time under the name requirements engineering. One long-running effort, the NaPiRE surveys, asks practitioners which requirements problems they actually run into. In one analysis, survey data from 228 organizations across 10 countries was used to identify the most critical requirements engineering problems, along with their causes and mitigation actions.2 The larger NaPiRE paper reports on 21 problems drawn from the literature, and studies their relevance and criticality in context.3

A narrower paper looked at one problem in two countries. Kalinowski and colleagues replicated the survey with 14 organizations in Austria and 74 in Brazil. They report that respondents from both countries cited the incomplete/hidden requirements problem as one of the most critical requirements engineering problems.1 In the Austrian data, that problem was named among the five most critical by 9 of the 14 participants.1

Notice what that problem is. It isn't a bad design or a clumsy implementation. It's that what somebody needed was never fully written down, or never surfaced at all.

## Why a gap in the spec is expensive

These studies describe people working with people: teams, customers, analysts. They say nothing about coding agents, and we won't claim they do. What follows is our reading, not a finding.

When you hand work to a colleague, a lot of the missing detail gets filled by shared context. They know the codebase, they know your taste, and they can walk over and ask. Even so, the respondents in these surveys, who work with people, still cited incomplete requirements as one of their most critical problems.

Delegating to a tool may remove some of that cushion, depending on what it can see and whether you can easily ask it questions. Either way, whatever you left out is a decision someone else now makes for you, often without telling you it was a decision.

## What a useful spec contains

A spec doesn't need to be long. It needs to settle the things you'd otherwise discover on review. Here's a short list we find holds up:

- The outcome. What should be true when this is done, in a sentence you could check.

- The boundaries. What's out of scope, and which files, interfaces or behaviors must not change.

- The reasons. Why this, why now, and what you already tried. Reasons let the other party make good calls on the cases you didn't foresee.

- The check. How you'll decide it worked: a test, a command, a screen you'll look at.

- The unknowns. What you haven't decided yet. Saying so beats leaving a silent hole.

Writing these down does something before anyone else reads them. It forces you to find the places where your own picture is blurry. Many of those places are invisible until you try to put them in a sentence.

## Specifying isn't the same as dictating

There's a fair worry that a detailed spec turns delegation into typing the code yourself. It doesn't have to. A good spec describes the destination and the constraints, not each step. You're deciding what, and leaving how to the person or tool doing the work.

It also won't be perfect. Requirements change as people learn. The aim isn't a complete document. It's to make the gaps visible early, while they're cheap to fill.

## Where a record helps

Cartographer reads the session history your coding agent already keeps and turns it into a map of how a project was built. Its prompt reading notes what each prompt anchors to, such as files, symbols, errors or pasted code, and it lets you declare with cartographer goal what done means, so each session is judged against that yardstick. Everything stays on your machine. Looking back, you can see where a hand-off was specific and where it was a hope.

## A habit worth trying

Before your next hand-off, write three lines: what done looks like, what's off limits, and how you'll check. If you can't write them, you've found the real next task. If you can, you've just made the work far easier for whoever picks it up, including future you.

## Sources

- Marcos Kalinowski, Michael Felderer, Tayana Conte, Rodrigo Spínola, Rafael Prikladnicki, Dietmar Winkler, Daniel Méndez Fernández and Stefan Wagner. Preventing Incomplete/Hidden Requirements: Reflections on Survey Data from Austria and Brazil. 8th Software Quality Days (SWQD), 2016.

- Mafra, Kalinowski, Méndez Fernández, Felderer and Wagner. Towards Guidelines for Preventing Critical Requirements Engineering Problems. Euromicro Conference on Software Engineering and Advanced Applications (SEAA), 2016. arXiv:1611.08833.

- Daniel Méndez Fernández, Stefan Wagner and 21 co-authors. Naming the Pain in Requirements Engineering: Contemporary Problems, Causes, and Effects in Practice. Empirical Software Engineering 22(5), 2017. arXiv:1611.10288.

Questions, or a topic you'd like us to dig into next? Reach out any time: mapit@codecartographer.dev. We read everything.
