# What a session transcript holds, and what it leaves out
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/blog/what-a-session-transcript-leaves-out
Description: A transcript records what was said and done, not why. Here's what research on design rationale says about the gap, and how to work with it.

Open an old session and you can read it like a ledger. Here's the prompt. Here's the reply. Here's the command that ran, the error that came back, the fix that followed. It's all there, in order, and it feels like a complete record.

Then you ask a different question. Why did we choose this approach and not the other one? And the ledger goes quiet. We wanted to spend this post on that quiet, because we think it's the most useful thing to understand about any record of work.

## A log holds events, not reasons

A transcript captures what was said and what was done. Reasons are a different kind of thing. They live in the head of whoever was deciding, and they only reach the page if that person happens to type them out.

Sometimes they do. A prompt might say "use the simple version, we only have two users." That's a reason, sitting in plain sight. More often the reason is a hunch, a half-remembered bug from last year, or a feeling that the last approach was getting too tangled. None of that gets typed. What gets typed is the instruction that came out the other end.

So the transcript shows the choice and hides the choosing. We can see that a dependency was swapped at 4:12 in the afternoon. We can't see the thing that made us tired of the old one.

## Software people have worried about this for a long time

The gap has a name in software engineering: design rationale, meaning the reasons behind a design. Researchers have studied whether people write it down and what stops them.

One survey of software practitioners, based on eighty-one valid responses, found that practitioners recognize the importance of documenting design rationale and frequently use it to reason about their design choices. The same survey also found that they reported barriers to using and documenting it.1 The authors started from the observation that there was little empirical evidence about how practitioners view rationale and how they document it.1

We find that comforting, in a way. People know the reasons matter. They use them. They still struggle to record them. If that's true of careful architects writing documents on purpose, it's no surprise that it's true of a chat window where the goal was to get something working.

## Some knowing doesn't turn into words

There's a deeper reason a log can't hold everything, and it's older than software. The philosopher Michael Polanyi opened his book on the subject with the idea that we can know more than we can tell.2 He called this the tacit dimension of knowing.

Most of us have felt it. You look at a function and sense it's wrong before you can say why. You prefer one name over another and can't defend it. Judgment like that steers a session, and it leaves almost no trace in the text. We'd be careful not to push the point further than it goes: Polanyi was writing about human knowledge in general, not about transcripts. But it's a fair reminder that a record of words can't be a record of everything that guided them.

## What a transcript is good for

None of this makes a transcript useless. It makes it a particular kind of evidence, and it helps to know which kind.

A transcript is strong on sequence. What came first, what came next, where the work stalled. It's strong on exact wording, including the moments you changed your mind. It's strong on friction: the error, the retry, the abandoned attempt. Those are things memory flattens quickly. A week later you'll remember that the thing worked. You won't remember the three tries it took.

It's weak on motive, on the options you considered and dropped silently, and on anything you knew without saying. If you read a transcript hoping for the why, you'll end up inventing one. That's the trap. A tidy story is easy to write after the fact, and it's easy to believe.

## Reading with the gap in mind

A few habits make a record more honest to read, whether it's yours or someone else's.

- Mark what's observed and what's inferred. "The prompt changed direction here" is observed. "Because the first approach felt wrong" is a guess.

- Look hardest at the corrections. A turn that starts with "no, not that" is a rare place where the reasoning surfaces, because you had to say what you wanted instead.

- When you're still in the work, write one line of why next to the what. It costs seconds and it's the thing the log can't supply later.

- Be willing to write "unknown" in the margin. An honest gap is more useful than a confident invention.

## Where a map fits

Cartographer reads the session history Claude Code already keeps, as one file per session, and turns it into a stream of events: prompts, replies, tools, errors and branch changes. It runs on your machine with no cloud. Every move it writes has to cite its evidence in the record, which keeps the telling tied to what happened and not to what sounds plausible. It can show you the sequence and the friction. The why you didn't say aloud stays yours to add.

## A record is a starting point

We think the healthiest way to hold a transcript is as a good witness who only saw part of the scene. It will tell you exactly what happened in the room. It won't tell you what anyone was thinking. For that, you still need the person, and a few honest notes while they still remember.

## Sources

- Antony Tang, Muhammad Ali Babar, Ian Gorton and Jun Han. A Survey of Architecture Design Rationale. Journal of Systems and Software.

- Michael Polanyi. The Tacit Dimension. First published 1966; University of Chicago Press edition.

Questions, or a topic you'd like us to dig into next? Reach out any time: support@codecartographer.dev. We read everything.

# Automation bias: what research says about trusting suggestions
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/blog/automation-bias-and-ai-suggestions
Description: Decades of human-factors research show people over-trust automated advice. Here's what it found, and what it means when you accept code suggestions.

Accepting a suggestion is cheap. A key press, and the code is in. That ease is the point of the feature, and it's also the thing human-factors researchers have been warning about for decades, in cockpits, control rooms and clinics. They have a name for it: automation bias.

## The classic experiment

In 1999, Linda Skitka, Kathleen Mosier and Mark Burdick published a study built on a simulated flight task. Some participants flew with a computer that monitored system states and made recommendations. Others flew without one. The researchers found that participants without automation outperformed those with a very reliable but not perfectly reliable aid on a monitoring task.1

The aid users also made two kinds of mistakes. They made omission errors, missing events when the aid didn't prompt them about it. And they made commission errors, doing what the automated aid recommended even when that contradicted other fully valid and available indicators.1

Read that twice. The aid wasn't bad. It was reliable. The trouble came from the small share of times it was wrong, because people had stopped watching for it.

## A broader picture

A decade later, Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey reviewed the empirical work in Human Factors. Their conclusion was that complacency and automation bias, which had often been studied apart, are different manifestations of overlapping automation-induced phenomena, with attention playing a central role.2

Two details from their abstract stand out. Automation bias shows up as omission and commission errors when decision aids are imperfect. And it isn't prevented by training or instructions.2 Knowing about the bias helps less than we'd like. Being told to stay alert doesn't reliably make anyone stay alert.

## What we can and can't say about code

These studies weren't about code suggestions, and we won't pretend they were. They looked at pilots-in-simulation and at automated aids in general. We also aren't making any claim about how any particular tool or model behaves. What follows is our own reading of the research, not a finding.

The shape of the problem does carry over. A suggestion is a piece of automated advice. You are the person deciding whether to act on it. The research says that when advice is usually right, attention drifts, and the rare wrong answer gets through. Two failure modes are worth watching for in your own work.

- Commission: you accept a suggestion that conflicts with something you already knew, such as a naming convention, a constraint from earlier in the project, or a failing test.

- Omission: you never notice what the suggestion left out, because nothing on the screen flags it. The missing error handling or the unconsidered edge case doesn't announce itself.

Omission is the harder one. A wrong line sits in front of you and can be read. An absent one can't.

## Habits that fit the research

Since instructions alone don't fix this, it helps to change the setup rather than rely on willpower. These are suggestions drawn from our reading, not proven remedies.

- Decide what you expect before you look. Write the one-line intent first, then compare the suggestion against it.

- Keep an independent check running. A test you wrote before the suggestion is a "fully valid indicator" that doesn't depend on the suggestion's own account of itself.

- Ask what's missing, not only what's wrong. Name one case the code should handle and look for it.

- Slow down on the easy ones. High reliability is exactly the condition under which attention drifts.

## Where a record helps

Cartographer reads the session history your coding agent already keeps and turns it into a map of how a project was built: what you asked, what happened, and how you responded. It reads what's already on your machine, with no cloud. If you want to see how often you accepted something without a pause, or where you stepped in and corrected course, that history is where the evidence lives.

## A fair reading

None of this says automated advice is bad. The aids in these studies were reliable, and that's why people leaned on them. The lesson is narrower. Trust that's calibrated to how often advice is right is sensible. Trust that stops checking isn't. The goal isn't to doubt every suggestion. It's to keep one part of your attention reserved for the times it's wrong.

## Sources

- Linda J. Skitka, Kathleen L. Mosier and Mark Burdick. Does automation bias decision-making? International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 51(5), 991-1006, 1999.

- Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich H. Manzey. Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration. Human Factors, 52(3), 381-410, 2010.

# What the docs say about giving a coding agent context
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/blog/what-the-docs-say-about-giving-an-agent-context
Description: Anthropic's docs and one study agree on a plain idea: context for a coding agent works best when it's short, specific and checked. Here's the close reading.

Ask ten developers how to set up a coding agent and you'll hear ten rituals. Write a huge instructions file. Paste in the whole architecture. Say it three times, in capitals. It's worth reading what the vendors actually put in writing, because the documentation is quieter than the advice around it. We read Anthropic's Claude Code documentation closely, and set it beside one recent study.

## Every session starts fresh

The starting point in Anthropic's documentation is a plain one: each Claude Code session begins with a fresh context window.1 Two mechanisms carry knowledge across sessions. One is CLAUDE.md files, which the docs describe as instructions you write to give Claude persistent context. The other is auto memory, which the docs describe as notes Claude writes itself based on your corrections and preferences.1

So whatever the agent knows about your project at the start of a session, it knows because something was loaded. Nothing carries over by itself.

## Context, not enforcement

The same page is careful about what these files can promise. It says Claude treats them as context, not enforced configuration.1 If you need an action blocked regardless of what Claude decides, the docs point to a PreToolUse hook instead. The best practices page makes the same split from the other side: CLAUDE.md instructions are advisory, while hooks are deterministic.2

That's a useful habit of mind. A line in an instructions file is a request, not a lock. If something must never happen, it needs a different mechanism than a sentence.

## Short, specific and pruned

The documentation's advice on length is consistent. The memory page says that the more specific and concise your instructions, the more consistently Claude follows them.1 The best practices page goes further and gives a test for every line: ask whether removing it would cause Claude to make mistakes, and if not, cut it. It warns that bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions.2

The same page lists what to leave out, including anything Claude can figure out by reading the code, and file-by-file descriptions of the codebase. It lists what to put in: commands Claude can't guess, style rules that differ from defaults, and architectural decisions specific to your project.2

The reasoning behind the pruning is the docs' main constraint. In their words, Claude's context window fills up fast, and performance degrades as it fills.2 Context isn't free storage. Everything you load competes for room with the work itself.

## Context also means a way to check

Not all context is background. The best practices page puts a different kind near the top: give Claude a way to verify its work, such as tests, a build, or a screenshot to compare.2 Their reasoning is that without a check the agent can run, "looks done" is the only signal available, and you become the verification loop.2

The page also recommends exploring and planning before coding, because letting Claude jump straight to coding can produce code that solves the wrong problem. It adds that if you could describe the diff in one sentence, you can skip the plan.2

## A study that fits the pattern

The vendor docs are guidance, not measurement. A 2026 paper by Thibaud Gloaguen and colleagues tested the idea directly on repository context files such as AGENTS.md. The authors report that context files increase inference cost by over 20%, and that agents tend to follow the instructions in them.3 Their conclusion is that unnecessary requirements make tasks harder, so human-written context files should describe only minimal requirements.3

The abstract's wording on task success differs between versions of the listing, so we won't summarize it here. Read the paper if that number matters to you. The cost and instruction-following findings are enough for our point.

## What we take from the reading

Three things stand out. First, the vendor and the researchers land in the same place: more context isn't better context. Second, the agent will tend to do what the file says, so every stale or unnecessary line is a small tax on every task. Third, a file is only as good as the last time someone checked it against reality.

That third point is ours, not the docs'. Treating the file like code, as Anthropic's page suggests, means reviewing it when things go wrong. But to review it, you need to remember what went wrong. Why did the agent ignore that rule? Which correction did you make three times?

That's where a session record helps. Cartographer reads the session history your coding agent already keeps and turns it into a map of how a project was built: what you asked, what happened, and how you responded. It reads what's already on your machine, with no cloud. The repeated corrections are right there when you sit down to edit the file.

## A short checklist, drawn from the docs

- Keep the instructions file short, and cut any line whose removal wouldn't cause a mistake.

- Put must-never-happen rules in a mechanism that enforces them, not in prose.

- Give the agent a check it can run, and ask for the evidence.

- Revisit the file when behavior surprises you, not on a schedule.

## Sources

- Anthropic. How Claude remembers your project. Claude Code documentation.

- Anthropic. Best practices for Claude Code. Claude Code documentation.

- Thibaud Gloaguen, Niels M&uuml;ndler, Mark M&uuml;ller, Veselin Raychev and Martin Vechev. Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents?. arXiv:2602.11988, 2026.
